item.title: Reverse-a-function drill — 2026-10-16
item.description:
Target: Windows x86-64 (args in `ecx`, `edx`; return in `eax`).
Reverse this short function to equivalent C:
```asm mystery: lea eax, [rcx+rcx*2] lea eax, [rdx+rax*4+7] ret ```
What does `mystery(int a, int b)` compute? No `imul`, `add` or `shl` appears, so where is the arithmetic happening?
## Answer
```c int mystery(int a, int b) { return 12 * a + b + 7; } ```
## Explanation
- `lea` runs the address-generation math `base + index*scale + disp` (scale 1/2/4/8) but never touches memory, so it works as a cheap multiply-add. - First `lea`: a + a*2 = 3a. Second: b + (3a)*4 + 7 = 12a + b + 7, three terms folded into one instruction. - Unlike `add`/`imul`, `lea` leaves the flags unchanged, which is why compilers love it; the 32-bit destination zero-extends into rax.
